questions.title: Contents attached to the anterior border of the pancreas
questions.question: ……… is one of the contents of the structure attached to the anterior border of the pancreas.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right gastric vessels run in the free edge of the lesser omentum along the lesser curvature of the stomach, not in the structure that attaches to the pancreas's anterior border.
explanations.B: Correct. The transverse mesocolon and the greater omentum's posterior layer attach along the anterior border of the pancreas, and the left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) vessels run within the layers of that attachment as they pass toward the greater curvature. This is why surgeons dividing the greater omentum off the transverse mesocolon near the pancreas must identify and protect these vessels. Recognising the anterior-border attachment as the transverse mesocolon/greater omentum root, and its contained vessel, is the key teaching point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hepatic artery runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum toward the porta hepatis, well away from the pancreas's anterior border attachment.
explanations.D: Incorrect, since only the left gastroepiploic vessels (not the right gastric vessels or hepatic artery) are contained in this specific attachment.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the transverse mesocolon/greater omentum attachment to the pancreas's anterior border and the vessels it carries.

questions.title: Paraumbilical vein dilatation in liver cirrhosis
questions.question: A 76-year-old male was followed in the gastroenterology unit because of alcoholic liver cirrhosis (ALC). A computerized tomography of the abdomen showed dilatation of the paraumbilical veins. What is the most likely vein to be obstructed?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The azygos vein is a systemic (caval) tributary at the oesophagus, not the vessel whose obstruction dilates the paraumbilical veins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The right branch of the portal vein does not communicate with the paraumbilical veins; the round-ligament (ligamentum teres) route that carries the paraumbilical veins runs from the left branch.
explanations.C: Correct. The paraumbilical veins run in the falciform ligament alongside the ligamentum teres (obliterated umbilical vein), draining into the left branch of the portal vein. In portal hypertension from cirrhosis, this portosystemic pathway dilates and can reopen, producing the paraumbilical/periumbilical varices seen on imaging as 'caput medusae' — so left portal-branch obstruction/hypertension is the vessel implicated, not the right branch.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The left gastric vein forms a different portosystemic anastomosis (with the oesophageal veins, producing oesophageal varices), not the paraumbilical pathway.

questions.learning_objective: Link paraumbilical vein dilatation in portal hypertension to the left branch of the portal vein via the ligamentum teres pathway.

questions.title: Inferior boundary of the epiploic foramen
questions.question: The inferior boundary of the structure that separates the portal vein from the IVC is…….

explanations.A: Incorrect. The common bile duct runs in the anterior (right free) margin of the epiploic foramen, alongside the portal vein and hepatic artery — it is a content of the anterior boundary, not the inferior boundary.
explanations.B: Correct. The epiploic foramen (of Winslow) — the only opening between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs — has the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct in its anterior boundary (free edge of lesser omentum) and the IVC in its posterior boundary. Its inferior boundary is the first (superior) part of the duodenum, which is why this landmark is used surgically to identify the foramen and control bleeding by compressing the structures within the free edge of the lesser omentum (Pringle manoeuvre).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The head of the pancreas lies inferior and to the right of the epiploic foramen but is not itself a named boundary of the foramen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior surface (visceral surface) of the liver forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen, not the inferior one.

questions.learning_objective: State the four boundaries of the epiploic foramen (of Winslow), including its inferior boundary.

questions.title: Portal vein termination and the lesser omentum
questions.question: The structure in which the portal vein terminates gives an attachment to:

explanations.A: Correct. The portal vein terminates at the porta hepatis (the hilum of the liver), where it divides into right and left branches before entering the liver substance. The porta hepatis is the site where the free edge of the lesser omentum attaches to the liver, carrying the portal triad structures into it — so the terminating structure (porta hepatis) is exactly where the lesser omentum attaches.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament connects the spleen to the left kidney and carries the splenic vessels and tail of pancreas — it has no attachment at the porta hepatis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The gastrophrenic ligament connects the fundus of the stomach to the diaphragm, unrelated to the porta hepatis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The greater omentum hangs from the greater curvature of the stomach and transverse colon; it does not attach at the porta hepatis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the porta hepatis as the site of portal vein termination and lesser omentum attachment.

questions.title: Posterior wall of the lesser sac
questions.question: The posterior wall of the structure separating the stomach from the pancreas is formed of:

options.C: Peritoneum covering upper part of abdominal aorta

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Peritoneum over the coeliac trunk is one of several structures forming the posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa), but it is not the only one — see D.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. Peritoneum over the left kidney and suprarenal gland also floors part of the lesser sac's posterior wall, but again is not the only contributor — see D.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. Peritoneum over the upper abdominal aorta likewise contributes to the posterior wall, but not exclusively — see D.
explanations.D: Correct. The lesser sac (omental bursa) lies behind the stomach and in front of the pancreas; its posterior wall is formed by peritoneum draped over several retroperitoneal structures in sequence — the diaphragmatic crura, the coeliac trunk and its branches, the left suprarenal gland and kidney, and the upper abdominal aorta — before the peritoneum reflects forward again over the anterior surface of the pancreas. All three listed structures are genuine components of that posterior-wall peritoneal covering.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the lesser sac (omental bursa) as the space separating the stomach from the pancreas and list the structures forming its posterior wall.

questions.title: Gastroduodenal junction and the pancreatic neck
questions.question: Gastroduodenal junction is related to…..

options.A: Anterior surface of neck of pancreas
options.B: Inferior surface of body of pancreas
options.C: Posterior surface of head of pancreas
options.D: Anterior surface of tail of pancreas

explanations.A: Correct. The pylorus (gastroduodenal junction) lies directly anterior to the neck of the pancreas, at roughly the level of L1. This relation is used clinically when locating the pancreatic neck intra-operatively via the pylorus, since the neck is the segment most directly reached by tracing posteriorly from the pyloroduodenal junction. It is also the landmark surgeons use to divide the pancreas at its narrowest point during a pancreaticoduodenectomy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior surface of the body of the pancreas relates to the duodenojejunal flexure and jejunal loops, not the gastroduodenal junction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior surface of the head of the pancreas relates to the IVC, right renal vessels and bile duct, not the pylorus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior surface of the tail of the pancreas relates to the splenic hilum region, well to the left of the gastroduodenal junction.

questions.learning_objective: State that the gastroduodenal junction (pylorus) lies anterior to the neck of the pancreas.

questions.title: Posterior relations of the pancreatic head
questions.question: All of the following are posterior to the head of pancreas except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true posterior relation, so not the exception). The IVC runs directly posterior to the head of the pancreas.
explanations.B: Correct. The superior mesenteric artery does not lie posterior to the head — it passes anterior to the uncinate process, between the head/uncinate process and the SMV, and continues inferior to the neck; it is a related structure but not a posterior one, making it the exception among these four. This anterior relation of the SMA to the uncinate process is exactly why an aggressive pancreatic head tumour can encase the SMA and render a resection unsafe.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true posterior relation, so not the exception). The right renal vessels (and the left renal vein crossing to the IVC) lie posterior to the pancreatic head.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true posterior relation, so not the exception). The lower part of the common bile duct is embedded in, or directly posterior to, the head of the pancreas before it joins the pancreatic duct.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the posterior relations of the pancreatic head (IVC, renal vessels, bile duct) from the SMA, which passes anterior to the uncinate process rather than posterior to the head.

questions.title: Arterial supply of the pancreas
questions.question: Blood supply branches of pancreas come from :

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. The coeliac trunk (via the splenic artery's pancreatic branches and the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery from the gastroduodenal artery) is one of two contributing sources — see D.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut (distal transverse colon to upper rectum) and has no branches to the pancreas.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. The superior mesenteric artery (via the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery) is the other contributing source — see D.
explanations.D: Correct. The pancreas straddles the foregut/midgut boundary, so it receives blood from both the coeliac trunk (splenic artery branches to the body/tail, and the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery to the head) and the superior mesenteric artery (via the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery to the head/uncinate process) — hence both A and C. This dual foregut/midgut supply also explains why a pancreatic head resection (Whipple procedure) must carefully preserve the SMA-derived arcade while the coeliac-derived vessels are divided.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pancreas is supplied by both the coeliac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery, reflecting its foregut/midgut position.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p3, Anatomy Q8

questions.title: Termination of the inferior mesenteric vein
questions.question: Inferior mesenteric vein terminates in the.......

explanations.A: Correct. The inferior mesenteric vein ascends retroperitoneally and typically drains into the splenic vein (behind the body of the pancreas), which then joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein — so the IMV's direct termination is the splenic vein, not the portal vein itself. Recognising this indirect route matters clinically, since splenic vein thrombosis can produce isolated (left-sided/sinistral) portal hypertension with gastric varices sparing the rest of the portal system.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The IMV reaches the portal vein only indirectly, via the splenic vein; it is the splenic-vein union with the SMV that forms the portal vein.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The left gastric vein drains the lesser curvature of the stomach and typically joins the portal vein or splenic vein directly, but it is not where the IMV terminates.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The IMV is a portal tributary and does not drain into the systemic IVC.

questions.learning_objective: State that the inferior mesenteric vein most commonly drains into the splenic vein, not directly into the portal vein.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p3, Anatomy Q9

questions.title: Portosystemic anastomosis at the anorectal junction
questions.question: In case of Liver cirrhosis, this may lead to portosystemic anastomosis at the lower end of anal canal between..........

options.A: Superior rectal vein and middle, inferior rectal veins
options.B: Left gastric vein and azygos vein
options.C: Right colic vein and right renal vein

explanations.A: Correct. In the wall of the lower rectum and anal canal, the superior rectal vein (a portal tributary, via the inferior mesenteric vein) anastomoses with the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic tributaries, draining via the internal iliac and internal pudendal veins). In portal hypertension this anastomosis can dilate, producing internal haemorrhoids.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The left gastric vein anastomoses with oesophageal veins (azygos system) at the gastro-oesophageal junction, producing oesophageal varices — a different portosystemic site, not the anal canal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The right colic vein is a portal tributary draining the ascending colon; it does not anastomose with the right renal vein, which is a purely systemic vessel.
explanations.D: Incorrect, since A correctly names the anorectal portosystemic anastomosis.

questions.learning_objective: Name the anorectal portosystemic anastomosis (superior rectal vein with middle/inferior rectal veins) and its clinical consequence in portal hypertension.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p3, Anatomy Q10

questions.title: Peritoneal covering of the pancreas — the tail
questions.question: Which part of pancreas is covered by peritoneum anteriorly and posteriorly :

explanations.A: Incorrect. The head of the pancreas is retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on its anterior surface.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The body of the pancreas is likewise retroperitoneal, with peritoneum on its anterior surface only.
explanations.C: Correct. Unlike the rest of the gland, the tail of the pancreas lies within the two layers of the lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament as it approaches the splenic hilum, so it is covered by peritoneum both anteriorly and posteriorly — making it the one part of the pancreas that is intraperitoneal in this sense, and mobile enough to be easily separated from the spleen surgically. This same peritoneal relationship is why the tail is the part of the pancreas most easily injured, or deliberately mobilised, during splenectomy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The neck of the pancreas is retroperitoneal, with peritoneum only on its anterior surface.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the tail of the pancreas as the only part covered by peritoneum on both surfaces, lying within the lienorenal ligament.

questions.title: Consequences of head-of-pancreas carcinoma
questions.question: Cancer of head pancreas leads to :

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. A pancreatic head mass causes post-hepatic (obstructive), not hepatocellular (hepatic), jaundice — see D.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone, though true — see D for the fuller answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone, though true — see D for the fuller answer.
explanations.D: Correct. A carcinoma of the pancreatic head commonly compresses the intrapancreatic part of the common bile duct as it passes through or behind the head, producing obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice, and can also compress the adjacent portal vein — which forms posterior to the pancreatic neck close to the head — as the tumour enlarges, so both B and C occur. Recognising both consequences together is what distinguishes a head-of-pancreas cancer vignette from a body/tail cancer, which is less likely to obstruct the duct so early.

questions.learning_objective: Explain how a head-of-pancreas carcinoma produces obstructive jaundice and portal vein compression through the head's close relations to the bile duct and portal vein.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p4, Anatomy Q12

questions.title: Portosystemic anastomosis around the umbilicus
questions.question: The portosystemic anastomosis around the umbilicus is formed by:

options.A: Left branch of portal vein & anterior abdominal wall veins.
options.B: Superior mesenteric vein & inferior vena cava.
options.C: Right colic vein & right renal vein.

explanations.A: Correct. The paraumbilical veins, running with the ligamentum teres from the left branch of the portal vein to the umbilicus, anastomose there with the small systemic veins of the anterior abdominal wall (superficial and inferior epigastric veins). This is the umbilical/periumbilical portosystemic anastomosis, which dilates in portal hypertension to give the classic 'caput medusae'.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior mesenteric vein is a purely portal vessel and does not anastomose with the systemic IVC at the umbilicus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The right colic vein (portal) and right renal vein (systemic) are unrelated to the umbilical anastomosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The left gastric vein anastomoses with oesophageal veins at the gastro-oesophageal junction — a different site, not the umbilicus.

questions.learning_objective: Name the umbilical portosystemic anastomosis (paraumbilical veins from the left portal branch with anterior abdominal wall veins) and its clinical sign (caput medusae).

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p4, Anatomy Q13

questions.title: Lymphatic drainage of the pancreatic head
questions.question: The upper part of the head of the pancreas drains into:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pancreaticosplenic nodes, along the splenic artery, mainly drain the body and tail of the pancreas, not the upper head.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Para-aortic nodes are a later downstream station, not the first-echelon drainage of the upper head.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Superior mesenteric nodes drain the lower part of the pancreatic head and uncinate process (following the inferior pancreaticoduodenal vessels), not the upper part.
explanations.D: Correct. Lymphatics from the upper part of the pancreatic head follow the superior pancreaticoduodenal vessels and the vessels along the pancreas's superior border to drain into the coeliac (pancreaticoduodenal/hepatic) group of nodes, consistent with the head's foregut-related arterial supply from the coeliac trunk via the gastroduodenal artery. In contrast, the lower head and uncinate process drain along the SMA-derived vessels to superior mesenteric nodes, so head-of-pancreas tumours can spread to either nodal group depending on exact location.

questions.learning_objective: State that the upper head of the pancreas drains to coeliac nodes, following its superior pancreaticoduodenal (coeliac-derived) blood supply.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p4, Anatomy Q15

questions.title: Arterial supply of the pancreatic head
questions.question: Which of the following arteries supplies the head of the pancreas?

explanations.A: Correct. The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, a branch of the gastroduodenal artery (from the coeliac trunk's common hepatic branch), runs along the head of the pancreas and anastomoses with the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery from the SMA — together forming the arcades that supply the head. Because both the coeliac-derived superior and SMA-derived inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries anastomose around the head, this arcade is a key anatomical basis for the dual (foregut and midgut) blood supply tested in question 8.
explanations.B: Incorrect as stated. The SMA itself does not directly supply the head; it does so only via its inferior pancreaticoduodenal branch, whereas the option listed here (A) is the more direct and specifically named supplying vessel.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pancreatic branches of the splenic artery supply the body and tail of the pancreas, not the head.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut and has no pancreatic branches.

questions.learning_objective: Name the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery as a principal supply to the pancreatic head, arising via the gastroduodenal artery from the coeliac trunk.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p5, Anatomy Q17

questions.title: Opening of the accessory pancreatic duct
questions.question: The accessory pancreatic duct opens in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The first part of the duodenum receives no named pancreatic duct opening.
explanations.B: Correct. The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) opens on the minor duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, proximal to (above) the major papilla where the main pancreatic duct joins the bile duct to open together. In most people the accessory duct communicates with the main pancreatic duct and drains a smaller volume, though in a minority (pancreas divisum) it becomes the dominant drainage route.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The third part of the duodenum has no pancreatic duct opening.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fourth part of the duodenum, leading to the duodenojejunal flexure, has no pancreatic duct opening.

questions.learning_objective: State that the accessory pancreatic duct opens at the minor duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p5, Anatomy Q18

questions.title: Inferior surface relations of the pancreas
questions.question: Inferior surface of the pancreas is related to all of the following, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true relation, so not the exception). The duodenojejunal flexure lies close to the inferior surface near the pancreatic body/tail.
explanations.B: Correct. The sympathetic chain lies on the posterior abdominal wall alongside the vertebral bodies, related to the posterior surface of the pancreas (along with the aorta, coeliac plexus and left kidney) rather than to its inferior surface — making it the exception among these four. Its presence there, rather than on the inferior surface, is what allows retroperitoneal spread of pancreatic cancer to produce severe back pain via splanchnic nerve invasion.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true relation, so not the exception). Loops of jejunum (the option's 'ilium' is a transcription of ileum/jejunum loops) lie inferior to the pancreas, in contact with its inferior surface.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true relation, so not the exception). The root of the transverse mesocolon and transverse colon relate to the inferior surface/anterior border of the pancreas.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the inferior-surface relations of the pancreas from its posterior relations (sympathetic chain, aorta, left kidney).

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p5, Anatomy Q19

questions.title: Where the portal vein forms
questions.question: Formation of the portal vein occurs at which part of the pancreas?

options.A: At the anterior surface of the body of pancreas.
options.B: At the superior border of the pancreas.
options.C: Anterior to the head of the pancreas.
options.D: Posterior to the neck of the pancreas.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior surface of the body is not the site of portal vein formation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior border of the pancreas relates to the splenic artery's course, not to portal vein formation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The SMA (not the portal vein) passes anterior to the uncinate process of the head.
explanations.D: Correct. The portal vein forms posterior (deep) to the neck of the pancreas, at approximately the level of L1-L2, by the union of the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein — a landmark surgeons use when assessing pancreatic neck resectability, since the vein lies directly behind this segment. Because the vein lies immediately behind this segment, ultrasound or CT assessment of the pancreatic neck-portal vein interface is a standard step in staging pancreatic cancer for resectability.

questions.learning_objective: Locate portal vein formation (splenic vein + SMV union) posterior to the neck of the pancreas.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p5, Anatomy Q20

questions.title: Distal ileum features
questions.question: Which of the following describes the distal 3/5 of the mobile part of small intestine

options.A: It has a thick wall and wide lumen
options.C: It has numerous and complex arcades

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ileum (the distal 3/5 of the jejuno-ileal loops) has a thinner wall and narrower lumen than the jejunum, the opposite of this statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ileal mesentery carries more fat than the jejunal mesentery, again the opposite of this statement.
explanations.C: Correct. The ileum's mesentery is characterised by numerous short, complex vascular arcades with several tiers of arterial loops, producing a dense arcade pattern, in contrast to the jejunum's fewer, longer, simpler arcades with long straight vasa recta. This dense arcading, together with a thinner wall and narrower lumen, is why the terminal ileum is the classic site for identifying bowel segment on both imaging and at laparotomy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ileum is distinguished by having numerous Peyer's patches (aggregated lymphoid follicles) in its antimesenteric wall, particularly in the terminal ileum — the opposite of this statement.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish jejunal from ileal mesenteric arcade pattern, wall thickness, mesenteric fat and Peyer's patch distribution.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p6, Anatomy Q21

questions.title: Structures crossed by the root of the mesentery
questions.question: All of the following structures crossed by root of mesentery except

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true crossing, so not the exception). The root of the mesentery, running obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal junction, crosses the IVC.
explanations.B: Incorrect (a true crossing, so not the exception). It crosses the right gonadal (testicular/ovarian) vessels.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true crossing, so not the exception). It crosses the right genitofemoral nerve on psoas major.
explanations.D: Correct. The oblique root of the mesentery crosses the third part of the duodenum, aorta, IVC, right ureter, right gonadal vessels, right genitofemoral nerve and right psoas major — all on the right side of the posterior abdominal wall — so it does not cross the left ureter, making that the exception. This right-sided course explains why right ureteric injury is a recognised risk during small bowel mesenteric surgery near this line, while the left ureter is comparatively protected.

questions.learning_objective: List the structures crossed by the oblique root of the mesentery, and recognise that they are right-sided (right ureter, not left).

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p6, Anatomy Q22

questions.title: Posterior relations of the caecum
questions.question: All of the following is true about posterior relations of caecum except

options.B: Medial cutaneous nerve of the thigh

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true posterior relation, so not the exception). Psoas major lies posterior to the caecum on the posterior abdominal wall.
explanations.B: Correct. The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, not the medial cutaneous nerve, runs on iliacus behind the caecum; the medial cutaneous nerve of the thigh instead arises from the femoral nerve within the thigh and has no posterior relation to the caecum, making this statement the exception. Distinguishing lateral from medial cutaneous nerve of the thigh distributions is a common source of confusion, since both nerves supply thigh skin but arise and course quite differently in relation to the caecum.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true posterior relation, so not the exception). Iliacus lies posterior to the caecum, continuous with psoas major.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true posterior relation, so not the exception). The femoral nerve, formed on psoas major, lies posterior to the caecum before it passes into the thigh.

questions.learning_objective: List the true posterior relations of the caecum (psoas major, iliacus, femoral nerve, lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh) and exclude the medial cutaneous nerve of the thigh.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p6, Anatomy Q23

questions.title: Appendicitis referred to the umbilical region
questions.question: A 24-year-old woman has a dull aching pain in the umbilical region, and flexion of the hip against resistance (psoas test) causes a sharp pain in the right lower abdominal quadrant. Which of the following structures is most likely inflamed to cause the pain?

explanations.A: Correct. Early visceral appendiceal pain is referred to the periumbilical region because the appendix's visceral afferents travel with sympathetic fibres back to the T10 spinal segment, which also supplies the umbilical dermatome; a positive psoas sign (pain on hip flexion against resistance) then localises inflammation to a retrocaecal/retroperitoneal appendix irritating psoas major, shifting the pain to the right iliac fossa as somatic (parietal peritoneal) pain takes over. This same T10 referral pattern is why the classic history describes pain that starts vaguely centrally before migrating and sharpening over the right iliac fossa as inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gallbladder (biliary) pain is typically referred to the right hypochondrium/right shoulder tip (via the phrenic nerve, C3-5), not the umbilicus, and does not produce a psoas sign.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pancreatic pain is typically epigastric with radiation to the back, not classically periumbilical with a positive psoas sign.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hepatic pain localises to the right hypochondrium, not the umbilical region, and is not associated with the psoas sign.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why early appendicitis is referred to the umbilical region (T10 visceral afferents) and how the psoas sign localises a retrocaecal appendix.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p6, Anatomy Q24

questions.title: Acute appendicitis diagnosis
questions.question: A 37-year-old woman was admitted to the emergency department with high fever (39.5° C), nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination revealed increased abdominal pain in the paraumbilical region, rebound tenderness over McBurney's point, Blood tests showed marked leukocytosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis

explanations.A: Correct. Fever, paraumbilical pain migrating to (or with rebound tenderness at) McBurney's point (the classic surface landmark for the base of the appendix, one-third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus), together with leukocytosis, is the textbook presentation of acute appendicitis. The combination of systemic signs (fever, leukocytosis) with a localising physical sign at McBurney's point is what pushes the diagnosis from 'possible' to 'most likely' appendicitis over the other options.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cholecystitis presents with right hypochondrial pain and a positive Murphy's sign, not tenderness at McBurney's point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal colic from a kidney stone presents with loin-to-groin colicky pain, not fixed tenderness at McBurney's point.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Duodenal perforation presents with sudden severe epigastric pain and peritonitis, not localised McBurney's point tenderness.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the clinical diagnostic pattern of acute appendicitis (fever, McBurney's point tenderness, leukocytosis).

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p6, Anatomy Q25

questions.title: Vessel ligated after post-appendectomy bleeding
questions.question: Two days after an appendectomy on a 45-year-old male patient, the patient has developed an elevated temperature (39° C), is hypotensive, and complains of abdominal pain. An exploratory laparotomy reveals large amounts of blood in the peritoneal cavity due to an injury to a vessel that occurred during the appendectomy. Which of the following vessels must be ligated to stop the bleeding?

options.C: Right colic a and superior rectal a

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon, not the appendix; it is not the vessel typically injured during appendectomy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ligating the SMA itself would devascularise the entire midgut, a drastic and inappropriate step for isolated bleeding after appendectomy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior rectal artery supplies the rectum, unrelated to the appendix or this bleeding source.
explanations.D: Correct. The appendicular artery — the vessel divided (and, if incompletely secured, the source of post-operative bleeding) during appendectomy — is an end artery arising from the ileocolic artery. Controlling the bleed after a slipped or inadequately ligated appendicular artery stump requires securing the ileocolic artery, its parent vessel.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the appendicular artery as a branch of the ileocolic artery, and its clinical significance in post-appendectomy haemorrhage.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p7, Anatomy Q26

questions.title: Jejunal characteristics
questions.question: Jejunum is characterized by all the following Except:

options.A: Its diameter has thick wall and wide lumen
options.B: Its mesentery has few fat and windows

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true jejunal feature, so not the exception). The jejunum has a thicker wall and wider lumen than the ileum.
explanations.B: Incorrect (a true jejunal feature, so not the exception). The jejunal mesentery is thin, with less fat and translucent 'windows' between vessels, unlike the fat-laden ileal mesentery.
explanations.C: Correct. Peyer's patches (aggregated lymphoid follicles) are a defining feature of the ileum, particularly the terminal ileum, not the jejunum — making this the exception among jejunal characteristics. Recognising this exception matters clinically, since it is the ileum's Peyer's patches — not any jejunal feature — that are implicated in typhoid ileal perforation and in some patterns of Crohn's disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true jejunal feature, so not the exception). The jejunal mucosa has tall, numerous circular folds (plicae circulares/valvulae conniventes), more prominent than in the ileum.

questions.learning_objective: List jejunal distinguishing features (thick wall, wide lumen, sparse mesenteric fat, numerous mucosal folds) and exclude Peyer's patches, an ileal feature.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p7, Anatomy Q27

questions.hold: Self-contradictory distractor set — 'All of the following are considered characteristic feature of large intestine ... Except: B (teniae coli length shorter than the length of large intestine)' — B describes the accepted anatomical fact (teniae are ~1/6 shorter than the colon they invest, which is exactly why sacculations/haustra form), so it reads as true rather than as the exception the printed key (28.b) marks it as; A, C and D are also each independently true statements, leaving no internally consistent false option. Likely an OCR-garbled or genuinely ambiguous distractor in the source ('The length of of tenia coli...'). Not authored.

questions.title: Caecum and the appendiceal opening
questions.question: All of the following are true about caecum except:

options.A: It's completely covered by peritoneum (freely mobile)
options.B: It is related posteriorly to Psoas major and femoral nerve
options.C: It is communicated with the appendix which opens into its posteromedial aspect superior to ileocecal opening
options.D: It's supplied by anterior and posterior caecal arteries

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true statement, so not the exception). The caecum is usually completely invested by peritoneum and is freely mobile, lacking a true mesentery in most individuals.
explanations.B: Incorrect (a true statement, so not the exception). Psoas major and the femoral nerve are genuine posterior relations of the caecum.
explanations.C: Correct. The appendix opens into the caecum's posteromedial aspect, but INFERIOR to (below) the ileocaecal opening, not superior to it — so describing it as superior is the false statement, making this the exception. Getting this orientation right matters surgically, since locating the ileocaecal junction is the standard way to trace along the caecum to find a retrocaecal or otherwise hidden appendix base.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true statement, so not the exception). The caecum is supplied by the anterior and posterior caecal arteries, branches of the ileocolic artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the appendix opens into the caecum's posteromedial wall inferior to the ileocaecal opening, not superior to it.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p7, Anatomy Q30

questions.title: Right groin pain and the caecum
questions.question: A 14 year old boy is complaining of pain on his right groin which of the following is most likely to be the source of pain

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ascending colon lies in the right lumbar/flank region, higher than the groin, so it is a less likely direct source of right groin pain.
explanations.B: Correct. The caecum occupies the right iliac fossa, immediately adjacent to the right groin (inguinal) region, so caecal pathology (including a low-lying or pelvic appendix) is the most likely source of pain localised to the right groin. This proximity is also why a low-lying or pelvic appendix, when inflamed, can present with pain that the patient localises to the groin rather than the classic right iliac fossa.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The transverse colon lies across the upper abdomen, well away from the groin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sigmoid colon lies in the left iliac fossa, the mirror-image region on the opposite side from the right groin.

questions.learning_objective: Localise the caecum to the right iliac fossa/groin region as the most likely source of right groin pain among the colon's parts.

field_notes.au: GIT Final compiled bank p8, Anatomy Q31

questions.title: Peritoneal covering of the large intestine's named parts
questions.question: According to colic peritoneal covering; ……… is completely covered while ……. Is covered anteriorly and from the sides

options.B: Ascending and descending colon/ Transverse colon

explanations.A: Incorrect alone, though true — see D for the complete answer, which also includes the sigmoid colon pairing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the relationship: the ascending and descending colon are covered anteriorly and laterally only (retroperitoneal), while the transverse colon is completely covered (intraperitoneal on a mesocolon) — the opposite of what this option states.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone, though true — see D for the complete answer, which also includes the transverse colon pairing.
explanations.D: Correct. Both the transverse colon and the sigmoid colon are suspended on their own mesocolons and so are completely covered by peritoneum (mobile, intraperitoneal), while the ascending and descending colon are secondarily retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on their anterior surface and sides, with a bare posterior area fixed to the posterior abdominal wall. Both A and C correctly state one half of this pairing, so together they give the full picture.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the intraperitoneal (mesocolon-suspended) transverse and sigmoid colon from the secondarily retroperitoneal ascending and descending colon.
